papers.title: Kiselev black hole from semiclassical gravity with conformal anomaly
papers.label: arXiv:2611.34026v1

summary.one_liner: Solves the semiclassical Einstein equations with both type-A and type-B conformal anomaly contributions for a special relation between central charges and the cosmological constant, obtaining an exact Kiselev-type black hole metric.
summary.plain: This paper studies how quantum effects of matter fields near a black hole can change the black hole's shape in spacetime. The authors include the "type-B" part of a quantum effect called the conformal anomaly, not just the "type-A" part that earlier work used. For one specific relation between the theory's central charges and the cosmological constant, they find the equations can be solved exactly, giving a black hole of the known Kiselev form.
summary.why: Quantum corrections from the conformal anomaly are a candidate way to modify black hole geometry near where classical gravity breaks down, so a closed-form solution is a useful reference point. The text presents this mainly as a stepping stone toward studying black holes under the full anomaly; its broader physical significance is not established in the text.
summary.background:
- Black hole: a region of spacetime whose gravity is so strong that nothing escapes; described by a metric (a formula for distances and times).
- Semiclassical gravity: Einstein's gravity with the average quantum stress-energy of matter fields added as a source.
- Conformal anomaly: a quantum effect where the trace of the stress-energy tensor does not vanish, even for massless fields, under rescaling of distances. It is split into type-A and type-B parts, with coefficients called central charges.
- Cosmological constant: a term in Einstein's equations describing a background energy that affects large-scale spacetime curvature.
- Kiselev black hole: a known family of black hole solutions surrounded by an energy-density field with a specific equation of state.
- Exact solution: a closed-form answer to the equations, as opposed to a numerical or approximate one.

papers.abstract: Investigating black hole physics in semi-classical gravitational theory is an interesting and important direction. When the backreaction of the conformal anomaly-induced effective stress-energy tensor is taken into account, the black hole spacetime can be largely altered which changes many properties of the black hole. In this work, rather than restricting our attention to the type-A anomaly, we incorporate the type-B anomaly and investigate how it modifies the spacetime structure obtained when only the type-A anomaly is considered. We find that for a specific relation between the central charges and the cosmological constant, the semiclassical Einstein equations can be solved analytically, yielding a metric that takes the exact form of the Kiselev black hole. After deriving the solution, we further discuss the properties of this new black hole solutions. Our work serves as an essential stepping stone for studying black hole geometries under the full conformal anomaly.

papers.title: The all-loop spectrum of GGK strings
papers.label: arXiv:2611.34619v1

summary.one_liner: Studies the non-perturbative spectrum of GGK theory (the non-relativistic limit of string theory on AdS5×S5), showing in light-cone and static gauges that the bosonic spectrum on several vacua matches free massive and massless scalars in AdS2 at all loops, and that the quantum correction to the classical energy vanishes under regularised Hurwitz series summation.
summary.plain: This paper looks at a simplified, non-relativistic version of string theory, a framework that describes tiny vibrating strings moving in a curved space. The authors work out the full set of possible energy levels for these strings, including quantum effects at every order of approximation. They find that, for the cases they study, the energies come from free particles in a lower-dimensional curved space, and that the quantum corrections cancel out, leaving only the classical energy.
summary.why: It tests a conjecture by de Leeuw, Fontanella and Nieto-García (arXiv:2403.09563) about this limit, and it bears on the broader question of how exactly solvable the spectrum of strings in AdS/CFT is. The reliance on regularised Hurwitz series for the vanishing correction is a technical choice whose broader physical meaning is not explained in the text, so its wider significance is uncertain.
summary.background:
- String theory: models in which particles are tiny one-dimensional strings whose vibrations give the particle spectrum.
- AdS5×S5: a specific curved background (five-dimensional anti-de Sitter space times a five-sphere) central to the AdS/CFT correspondence.
- Non-relativistic limit: a simplified regime where the speed of light is effectively taken to be large, so the theory becomes easier to solve.
- GGK string: a string solution in this non-relativistic limit, studied here.
- Light-cone and static gauge: choices of coordinates that remove redundant freedom in describing the string.
- Vacuum and classical energy: a stable lowest-energy configuration of the string and its energy before quantum effects.
- All-loop / quantum correction: effects from quantum fluctuations summed over all orders of approximation.
- AdS2 scalar fields: particles of spin zero living in a two-dimensional anti-de Sitter space.
- Hurwitz series regularisation: a mathematical technique for assigning finite values to divergent sums.

papers.abstract: We study the non-perturbative spectrum of the non-relativistic limit of string theory in AdS$_5\times$S$^5$, also known as GGK theory. In light-cone gauge, we show that the bosonic spectrum on a number of vacua is described at all-loops by free massive and massless scalar fields in AdS$_2$, confirming a conjecture by de Leeuw, Fontanella and Nieto-Garc\'ia, arXiv:2403.09563. In static gauge, we obtain the same result for any classical string vacuum, and including fermions. We compute the quantum correction to the classical energy, and show that it vanishes once we adopt the regularised Hurwitz series. We conclude that the quantum energy spectrum built upon any GGK string consists solely of its classical vacuum energy.

papers.title: Free hyperboloidal evolution in 3D: gauge waves and constraint-violating gravitational waves
papers.label: arXiv:2611.31379v1

summary.background:
- General relativity describes gravity as the curvature of spacetime; numerical relativity solves its equations on computers.
- Gravitational waves are ripples in spacetime produced by accelerating massive objects.
- "Minkowski spacetime" is empty, flat spacetime, the simplest test background.
- "Future null infinity" is the idealized far-away region where outgoing light and gravitational waves end up; hyperboloidal slices are time slices that reach it.
- Conformal compactification maps infinite distance onto a finite boundary so the whole region can be simulated.
- BSSN and Z4 are standard formulations of Einstein's equations used in simulations; "free evolution" means the constraint equations are not enforced exactly during the run, so small constraint violations can appear.
- Gauge waves are coordinate-choice disturbances that do not carry physical energy.
summary.one_liner: This paper extends hyperboloidal (conformally compactified) evolution with the BSSN/Z4 formulation of general relativity from spherical symmetry to full 3D, demonstrating free evolution of gauge waves and constraint-violating gravitational waves on Minkowski spacetime with signal extraction at future null infinity.
summary.plain: Scientists who simulate gravity on computers usually have to cut off their simulated universe at a finite distance, which can distort the gravitational waves they want to study. This paper describes a way to carry the simulation all the way out to "future null infinity," the far-away boundary where outgoing waves can be read off cleanly, and it does so for full three-dimensional simulations. The authors test it on simple disturbances in empty flat space and report that the code runs reliably and the signals can be extracted at that far boundary.
summary.why: Clean access to waves at infinity matters for predicting the gravitational-wave signals that detectors such as LIGO and Virgo are meant to catch, so a working 3D tool is a useful building block. The text only covers tests in flat spacetime with simple perturbations, so it does not yet show how the method performs for realistic sources such as merging black holes.

papers.abstract: Hyperboloidal evolution allows to reach future null infinity within numerical relativity simulations. This work extends the conformal compactification approach with BSSN/Z4 from spherical symmetry to full 3D simulations. This is the first free numerical hyperboloidal evolution in 3D with a common formulation of general relativity. In this first step, gauge waves and constraint-violating gravitational waves perturbing Minkowski spacetime are evolved nonlinearly and show that the implementation is reliable and signals can be successfully extracted at future null infinity.

papers.title: NS5-branes and the black hole/string transition
papers.label: arXiv:2611.31945v1

summary.background:
- BTZ black hole: a simple black hole solution in three-dimensional spacetime, used as a toy model in gravity research.
- Supergravity solution: a classical geometry of gravity that solves the equations of a supersymmetric theory, often used to model string theory objects.
- BPS state: a special, highly symmetric configuration whose energy is fixed by its charges, making it easier to analyse.
- Fundamental string and NS5-brane: basic extended objects in string theory; branes are higher-dimensional generalisations of points or strings.
- Little strings: non-gravitational strings that live on NS5-branes and behave as the basic non-abelian degrees of freedom in the relevant theory.
- Deconfinement transition: a phase change, analogous to melting, in which the constituents of a bound state become free.
- D-string soliton: a stable, particle-like lump of energy built from D-strings, a class of branes that carry charge for open strings.
summary.one_liner: The paper extends a family of 6d BPS supergravity solutions (fundamental strings plus NS5-branes near the BTZ black hole threshold) to include gauge excitations of the fivebranes, and studies the energetics of D-string solitons relative to the deconfinement transition of little strings.
summary.plain: This paper is about a theoretical question in string theory: when does a tangle of strings turn into a black hole, and what happens at the tipping point between the two. The authors build more detailed model geometries that describe a set of strings and five-dimensional membranes (fivebranes) sitting very close to that tipping point. They then examine how much energy certain small objects called D-string solitons carry, and how that relates to the point where the little strings stop being confined.
summary.why: The black hole/string transition is a long-standing topic linking gravity and string theory, so the work matters to specialists studying that connection. The provided text only gives the aims and setup, not the specific results, so its broader significance is unclear from this summary alone.

papers.abstract: Near to the onset of BTZ black hole formation in string theory is a large ensemble of 6d BPS supergravity solutions sourced by slightly separated fundamental strings and Neveu-Schwarz fivebranes. We extend the construction of these geometries to include gauge excitations of the fivebranes, and then study the energetics of D-string solitons in relation to the deconfinement transition of little strings, which are the natural non-abelian degrees of freedom that deconfine in the transition to the black hole phase.

papers.title: Constraining Regular Black Hole Models with the Effective Field Theory treatment of General Relativity
papers.label: arXiv:2611.30616v1

summary.background:
- General relativity: Einstein's theory of gravity, in which mass bends spacetime; the Schwarzschild metric describes a non-rotating black hole.
- Singularity: a point where the classical equations break down, with curvature becoming infinite at the centre of a standard black hole.
- Regular black hole: a modified metric in which the centre is smooth and free of singularity, often proposed as a stand-in for quantum gravity effects.
- Metric: the mathematical rule giving distances and time intervals in spacetime.
- Effective field theory: treating a theory as valid only up to some energy scale, using corrections organised in powers of that scale; here it gives small, calculable quantum corrections.
- Perturbative vs non-perturbative: perturbative calculations expand in a small parameter; non-perturbative approaches aim to capture effects beyond such expansions.
summary.one_liner: The paper uses the known perturbative quantum correction to the static-particle interaction energy near a black hole, derived from treating general relativity as an effective field theory, as a test that non-perturbative "regular" (modified Schwarzschild) black hole metrics must satisfy, and applies it to the Hayward metric.
summary.plain: Physicists want to know what happens inside black holes once quantum effects of gravity are included, and one family of proposed answers is "regular" black holes, which replace the central singularity with a smooth core. This paper offers a way to check such proposals against a quantum correction that can be calculated with the well-established perturbative approach to gravity. The authors find that the Hayward model does not match this check, and they identify the most general modified metric that would reproduce the expected result.
summary.why: Regular black hole models are widely studied as possible outcomes of quantum gravity, but they are often hard to compare with anything firm. A concrete consistency test tied to a perturbative calculation gives a way to rule models in or out, though the text does not show how far this test reaches beyond the Hayward case.

papers.abstract: In this paper, we present a method for using perturbative predictions from treating general relativity as an effective field theory to constrain non-perturbative approaches to quantum gravity in black hole contexts. We start by reviewing a known result from this framework, which estimates the first quantum corrections to the interaction energy of a static particle near a black hole. We then propose a way to test non-perturbative quantum black hole models - specifically those formulated as modified Schwarzschild metrics, also known as regular black holes - against this perturbative result. To illustrate, we apply our method to the Hayward metric, showing that it does not align with the perturbative prediction, and we identify the most general metric that can reproduce the expected result.

papers.title: For whom the Bell tolls: joint measurements and state updates in quantum field theory
papers.label: arXiv:2611.30468v1

summary.background:
- Quantum field theory: a description where particles are excitations of fields spread through spacetime.
- Smeared field operator A(f): a field measured with a weighting function f over a region, rather than at a single point.
- Fewster-Verch framework: a rigorous way to describe measurements and state updates in curved spacetime quantum field theory.
- Bell inequality and CHSH: a test of whether measurement correlations can be explained by local hidden variables; quantum mechanics can exceed the classical limit, up to Tsirelson's bound.
- Fock space: the standard mathematical space of states containing variable numbers of particles.
- Normal and commuting operators: technical conditions meaning the measurements can be performed together and their outcomes are well defined jointly.
- Moment generating functional: a tool that encodes all the statistics (averages, spreads) of a distribution in one object.
- Proca field: a massive vector (spin-1) field, used here to model polarization.
summary.one_liner: The paper derives the joint probability distribution of commuting, normal smeared-field observables of the form A(f_i)*A(f_i) in the Fewster-Verch measurement framework (under assumed Fock-space representability), and uses it to build a CHSH Bell-test model with a coupled Proca-scalar polarization setup that violates the CHSH inequality up to Tsirelson's bound in the limit of perfect vacuum-effect rejection.
summary.plain: This paper asks how measurements in quantum field theory, the framework describing particles and fields, update the quantum state and whether those updates can produce the strong, "quantum" correlations seen in Bell tests. The authors compute the full joint statistics of several measurements of a field at once, under stated technical assumptions. They then build a simple Bell-test model based on a previously developed polarization model and report that it can exceed the CHSH limit, approaching the maximum allowed by quantum mechanics when background vacuum effects are removed.
summary.why: It shows that the state-update rules of a rigorous measurement framework for quantum fields are compatible with strongly nonclassical correlations, which matters for foundations of quantum field theory and quantum information. The reach beyond this model is unclear from the abstract alone, and the result depends on the stated assumptions and on the idealisation of perfect vacuum rejection.

papers.abstract: State update rules and their behaviour in Bell tests play an important role in the study of measurement schemes and quantum information. We consider the state updates of the Fewster-Verch measurement framework for quantum field theory using their connection to the probability distribution of measurement outcomes. We focus on a set of observables of the form $A(f_i)^*A(f_i)$, where $A(f)$ is the (complex) smeared field operator for any theory induced by a formally hermitian, Green hyperbolic differential operator, and where the $(A(f_i))_{i=1, \dots, m}$ are assumed to be normal and mutually commuting. Under the assumption that these operators have a sufficiently nice representation on a bosonic Fock space, we derive the joint moment generating functional and the unique joint probability distribution for the observables $(A(f_i)^*A(f_i))_{i=1,\dots,m}$. As an application of these results, we construct a model of a Bell inequality test within quantum field theory using a recently developed coupled Proca-scalar model for polarization measurements. We show that our Bell test model can violate the CHSH inequality, approaching Tsirelson's bound for maximally entangled states in the limit where vacuum effects are perfectly rejected. These results show that the state update rules derived in the Fewster-Verch framework are compatible with strongly quantum correlations. They also support a viewpoint in which state updates should be understood in relation to available information.

papers.title: Type-II quasinormal modes of dilaton--Euler--Heisenberg AdS black holes
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27195v1

summary.background:
- A black hole's quasinormal modes are damped oscillations with a real frequency (pitch) and an imaginary part (how fast they fade); negative imaginary part means stability.
- AdS (anti-de Sitter) is a universe with negative curvature that acts like a box confining signals.
- The dilaton is a hypothetical scalar field coupled to electromagnetism, appearing in some string-inspired gravity theories.
- Euler–Heisenberg corrections are nonlinear modifications to electromagnetism at strong fields, from quantum vacuum effects.
- ℓ is the angular-momentum label of a mode: ℓ=0 monopole, ℓ=1 dipole, ℓ=2 quadrupole.
- Chebyshev pseudospectral methods are numerical techniques for solving the governing equations accurately.
- A thermodynamic phase transition is a qualitative change in a system's state (like water boiling); here it is studied in the black hole's isobaric (constant-pressure) process.
summary.one_liner:
Computes Type-II quasinormal modes (coupled gravitational, dilaton and electromagnetic perturbations for ℓ=0,1,2) of a magnetically charged dilaton–Euler–Heisenberg black hole in AdS, using direct integration and Chebyshev pseudospectral methods, and links the ℓ=0 dilaton modes to the black hole's thermodynamic phase transition.</one_liner>
<parameter name="plain">The paper studies how a charged black hole in a curved, AdS-type universe "rings" after being disturbed, the way a struck bell rings at certain tones that fade over time. It looks at several coupled kinds of disturbance (gravity, a scalar "dilaton" field, and electromagnetism) and computes the tones and fading rates numerically. It reports that the black hole appears stable, since all modes it computes decay, and that the fading rate shows a change near the black hole's thermodynamic phase transition.
summary.why: Quasinormal modes are the characteristic signals a black hole emits when perturbed, so they are a theoretical handle on black-hole stability and on how such objects might be probed. The link drawn between these modes and a thermodynamic phase transition is the most unusual part; the text does not say how directly this could be tested, so the broader significance is uncertain.

papers.abstract: In this paper, we investigate Type-II quasinormal modes (QNMs) of a magnetically charged dilaton--Euler--Heisenberg black hole in anti-de Sitter (AdS) spacetime. The Type-II includes coupled gravitational, dilaton and electromagnetic perturbations. Its coupled equations are derived for $\ell=0,1,2$ modes and the QNM frequencies are calculated by employing direct integration and Chebyshev pseudospectral methods, giving consistent results. For nondegenerate dipole ($\ell=1$) mode at fixed curvature, the nonlinear correction starts at order $Q^2$ for electromagnetic-led branch and at order $Q^4$ for scalar-led branch. In this case, stronger AdS curvature enhances reduction of the electromagnetic-led real frequency for positive coupling, while gravitational-led quadrupole real frequency changes weakly with charge. As the curvature weakens, the dipole frequencies approach the AdS normal-mode scale and their damping decreases. We find that all modes computed have negative imaginary parts for nonextremal black holes, implying this black hole is stable against Type-II perturbations. Furthermore, we explore the connection between thermodynamic phase transition and QNMs for $\ell=0$ dilaton. For a subcritical isobaric process, the QNM real frequency of $\ell=0$ dilaton decreases with increasing temperature of small black holes, while it increases with increasing temperature of large black holes. At coexistence, the damping rate for large black holes is about 4.28 times that for small black holes.

papers.title: Onset of quantum chaos in a family of two-dimensional conformal field theories
papers.label: arXiv:2611.26694v1

summary.background:
- Conformal field theory (CFT): a quantum theory on a 2D surface that is scale-invariant; its states have "scaling dimensions," which act like energy levels.
- Sigma model with K3 target space: a 2D theory whose fields live on the K3 surface, a special four-dimensional shape from geometry.
- Supersymmetry (N=(4,4)): an extra symmetry relating bosons and fermions.
- Orbifold: a space made by quotienting a simpler space (here a torus) by a symmetry; the Kummer point is one such special point.
- BPS operators: protected states whose energies do not change under deformation; non-BPS ones can shift.
- Marginal deformation: a small change to the theory that does not change its scale-invariance at leading order.
- Degenerate levels and first-order splitting: several states with equal energy that separate under a small perturbation; the size of the separation at leading order is what is measured.
- Random matrix theory and GOE: statistics of eigenvalues of random symmetric matrices, used as the benchmark for chaotic quantum systems; diagnostics include gap ratios and rigidity.
summary.one_liner: In a family of two-dimensional K3 sigma models near the Kummer orbifold point, the first-order splitting of degenerate non-BPS spin-zero operator dimensions along generic blow-up deformation directions follows GOE random-matrix statistics once exact symmetries are resolved, unlike the singlet deformation.
summary.plain: This paper studies a quantum field theory on a two-dimensional surface, a sort of idealized model of string theory on a special shape called K3. At a special point the energy levels of certain particle-like states sit exactly on top of one another. The authors nudge the model in small directions and measure how these tied levels split apart, and find that the pattern of splittings looks statistically like the random-matrix patterns seen in complicated physical systems.
summary.why: Random-matrix statistics are a sign of quantum chaos, and finding them in a solvable conformal field theory is a question of interest for how chaos arises in quantum gravity-related models. The text supports the comparison with the singlet deformation, but whether this connects to broader holographic or gravitational questions is not established by the abstract alone.

papers.abstract: We exhibit random matrix statistics in the scaling dimensions of non-BPS primary operators in a family of two-dimensional conformal field theories. Specifically, we consider the sigma model with K3 target space and $\mathcal N=(4,4)$ supersymmetry in a neighborhood of the Kummer orbifold point $\mathbb T^4/\mathbb Z_2$. At the free-fermion radius, the spin-zero spectrum of the $\mathbb Z_2^4$-invariant sector is exactly degenerate at integer energies. The exactly marginal blow-up deformations that preserve this symmetry form a four-dimensional space, whose directions we parametrize by unit quaternions. Along each deformation direction, we compute the first-order splitting of the degenerate levels, i.e., the leading anomalous dimensions as the coupling goes to zero. In sectors where all exact symmetries are resolved, including a hidden $\mathbb Z_2$ at the even levels, the non-zero first-order shifts along a generic direction follow the Gaussian orthogonal ensemble (GOE), as we verify by computing several spectral diagnostics. We compare quantitatively with the well-known singlet deformation, which has enhanced symmetry: even after all its known symmetries are resolved, its first-order spectrum has exact degeneracies, its gap ratio approaches the GOE value only slowly as the energy increases, and its unfolded spectrum lacks the long-range rigidity of the GOE.

papers.title: Bianchi cosmologies with four-dimensional groups of motion in New General Relativity
papers.label: arXiv:2611.26474v1

summary.background:
- General Relativity: Einstein's theory of gravity, in which gravity is curvature of spacetime.
- Teleparallel gravity: an equivalent-style reformulation that describes gravity using torsion (a twisting of the geometry) instead of curvature.
- New General Relativity: a one-parameter family of teleparallel theories; the parameter selects a particular member of the family.
- Bianchi types: classes of spatially uniform but possibly anisotropic (direction-dependent) universe models, labelled by roman numerals.
- Symmetry group of motion: a set of transformations (such as translations and rotations) that leave the universe unchanged; more symmetries mean fewer free functions.
- Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker (FLRW) cosmology: the standard isotropic model of an expanding universe.
- Free functions of time: unknown quantities depending on time that the equations determine.
summary.one_liner: Derives and partially solves the field equations of one-parameter New General Relativity (a teleparallel gravity theory) for spatially homogeneous Bianchi II, III and IX universes that have a four-dimensional symmetry group.
summary.plain: This paper studies model universes that look the same everywhere in space, described by a rival formulation of gravity called New General Relativity, which describes gravity through a different geometric bookkeeping than Einstein's theory. The authors write down the most general versions of three such universe shapes (Bianchi types II, III and IX) that keep a four-dimensional set of symmetries, and derive the equations that govern them. They then present some solutions, finding some that resemble the standard expanding universe of Einstein's theory and some that deviate from it.
summary.why: Testing whether alternative formulations of gravity give cosmologies that differ from General Relativity is a way to probe what observations could distinguish them. The text does not indicate any direct link to observational data, so the practical significance is uncertain from this abstract alone.

papers.abstract: We study the dynamics of the most general metric teleparallel spacetimes of Bianchi types II, III and IX, which admit a four-dimensional symmetry group, in the 1-parameter family of New General Relativity. We first show that in each of these classes the most general metric teleparallel geometry is described by four free functions of time, while another four functions of time describe the most general energy-momentum tensor compatible with the same symmetries. We then derive the field equations of New General Relativity for this class of geometries. Finally, we present some solutions to these field equations. Our results show that both solutions resembling features of the standard Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker cosmology of General Relativity and deviations thereof exist.

papers.title: From Integrability to Chaos in Tensionless AdS3 String Theory
papers.label: arXiv:2611.25576v1

summary.background:
- AdS3×S3×T4 is a specific string theory background; AdS is a curved space with negative curvature, and holography relates it to a lower-dimensional quantum theory on its boundary.
- Tensionless string theory: a limit where the string's tension (stiffness) goes to zero, making the theory tractable.
- Symmetric product orbifold Sym^N(T^4): a conformal field theory built from N copies of a four-torus theory with copies permuted; it is the proposed dual description.
- Planar limit: the leading-order approximation where only the simplest interactions count, analogous to the leading term in a large-N expansion; non-planar corrections are the subleading ones.
- R-R flux: a background field (Ramond-Ramond) threaded through the bulk space.
- Integrability vs. chaos: integrable systems have many conserved quantities and regular spectra; chaotic systems show level repulsion and random-matrix-like spacing statistics.
- Level spacing statistics: the study of gaps between neighboring energy levels, used as a fingerprint of chaos.
summary.one_liner: The paper studies non-planar (quantum-gravitational) corrections to the integrable planar structure of the symmetric product orbifold Sym^N(T^4), dual to tensionless string theory on AdS3×S3×T4 with R-R flux switched on, and examines level spacing statistics for signs of random-matrix behavior.
summary.plain: This paper asks how a highly structured, exactly solvable model of string theory becomes chaotic once quantum gravity effects are included. The authors add a deformation that turns on a background field in the bulk (the higher-dimensional space) and look at how the energy levels are spaced. They report that the leading corrections break the exact degeneracies of the simple planar model and show some signs of the spacing patterns typical of random matrices.
summary.why: It offers a concrete, controlled setting in which string interactions are argued to drive the onset of quantum chaos, which is a question of interest across quantum gravity and holography. The text itself is limited to an abstract, so the strength of the evidence and how far the result generalizes are not something I can judge from it.

papers.abstract: We study quantum-gravitational corrections to the planar integrable structure of the symmetric product orbifold $\text{Sym}^N(\mathbb{T}^4)$ that is dual to tensionless string theory on AdS$_3\times$S$^3\times \mathbb{T}^4$. We consider the deformation that switches on R-R flux in the bulk, and analyze the associated level spacing statistics. The leading non-planar corrections lift the planar degeneracies and produce signs of random-matrix behavior. Our results provide a controlled example of string interactions driving the onset of quantum chaos.

papers.title: Long lived QNM for multiple black holes
papers.label: arXiv:2611.24063v1

summary.background:
- Black hole "ringing" (quasinormal modes): damped oscillations a black hole gives off after being disturbed, each with a characteristic frequency and decay rate.
- Extremal black hole: a black hole with the largest charge or spin allowed for its mass, which here makes several of them can sit in equilibrium together.
- Majumdar–Papapetrou spacetime: an exact solution of Einstein's equations describing several charged black holes in static balance.
- Null geodesic: the path light takes through curved spacetime.
- Trapped set: the set of light paths that neither escape to infinity nor fall into a black hole.
- Elliptic (stable) orbit: a light path that stays bounded and returns near itself, like a stable planetary orbit; such orbits are why ringing decays slowly.
- Exponential convergence to the real axis: the modes' decay rates shrink toward zero very quickly, meaning long-lived ringing.
summary.one_liner: The paper gives a rigorous definition of quasinormal modes for Majumdar–Papapetrou spacetimes containing several extremal black holes, and shows that for two equal-mass holes, stable elliptic orbits in the trapped set produce quasinormal modes that approach the real axis exponentially fast.
summary.plain: When a black hole is disturbed, it "rings" like a bell at characteristic frequencies, called quasinormal modes, which fade away over time. This paper studies that ringing for a model universe containing several extremal (maximally charged) black holes rather than just one. The authors give a precise mathematical definition of these modes for this setting and find that, for two equal-mass holes, some light paths can circle stably between them, which yields ringing that decays very slowly.
summary.why: The text describes this as the first mathematical result on quasinormal modes for multiple black holes, which is why it is notable within a field that has mostly studied single black holes. The text does not say how these results would be checked against observations of gravitational waves, so any link to astronomy is unclear from this abstract alone.

papers.abstract: We provide a rigorous definition of quasinormal modes (QNM) for the Majumdar--Papapetrou spacetimes with multiple extremal black holes. For certain configurations, the trapped set of the null geodesic flow contains stable (elliptic) orbits. We analyze this phenomenon in the case of two black holes of equal mass and show that it produces QNM converging exponentially fast to the real axis. QNM for black holes have been extensively studied for $\textit{single}$ black holes and this appears to be the first $\textit{mathematical}$ result for the case of multiple black holes.

papers.title: Nonzero cubic Love numbers of Schwarzschild black holes
papers.label: arXiv:2611.25059v1

summary.background:
- Tidal Love number: a number measuring how much an object deforms under an external tidal field; it characterises its internal response.
- Schwarzschild black hole: the simplest non-spinning, non-charged black hole in General Relativity.
- Linear, quadratic, cubic order: successively higher powers of the tidal strength; nonlinear effects enter at quadratic and cubic order.
- Worldline effective field theory (EFT): a method that treats a compact object as a point particle with extra terms describing its internal response, letting calculations be organised systematically.
- Dimensional regularization: a mathematical technique for handling divergent intermediate integrals by temporarily working in a non-integer number of dimensions.
- "Runs": a coupling that depends on the energy or length scale used in calculations; a non-running value is scale-independent.
- Octupolar: a tidal pattern with angular structure of degree three, more complex than the simple quadrupolar pattern.
summary.one_liner: The paper computes a cubic-order static Love number for Schwarzschild black holes under a non-axisymmetric octupolar tidal field, matching the result to a worldline effective field theory using dimensional regularization, and reports a nonzero value that neither vanishes nor runs with scale.
summary.plain: The paper asks how a black hole responds when it sits in an external gravitational "squeeze" that is stronger than the simple linear case. Earlier work found that a non-spinning black hole's static response vanishes at the first two orders, so the authors looked at the third order for one specific lopsided, non-symmetric pattern of squeezing. They report that the response at this order is nonzero and does not change with the mathematical scale used in the calculation.
summary.why: Love numbers describe how easily an object deforms under tides, and they can be read off from gravitational-wave signals of merging compact objects. A nonzero, scale-independent cubic value is notable because the text calls it surprising, but the text does not show how it would feed into observations, so its practical reach is unclear.

papers.abstract: Static Love numbers of Schwarzschild black holes vanish at linear and quadratic order in General Relativity, while generic nonlinear tides remain less understood. We solve a specific non-axisymmetric octupolar tide at cubic order and, building on the symmetry of static General Relativity exploited by Parra-Martinez and Podo, match the result to a worldline effective field theory (EFT) using dimensional regularization. Surprisingly, we find a Love number that neither vanishes nor runs.

papers.title: Comment on "Exact, nonsingular black holes from a phantom DBI field as primordial dark matter"
papers.label: arXiv:2611.23597v1

summary.background:
- Black hole: a region of spacetime from which nothing, including light, can escape, bounded by an event horizon.
- Singularity: a point where the curvature of spacetime becomes infinite and standard physics breaks down; "nonsingular" means avoiding this.
- General relativity: Einstein's theory linking spacetime geometry (the metric) to energy and matter.
- Scalar field: a field with a single value at each point in space, used in many dark matter and cosmology models.
- Dirac-Born-Infeld (DBI) field: a nonlinear scalar field theory, originally from string theory, with a built-in maximum speed for its dynamics; "phantom" refers to a sign choice giving negative energy density.
- Field equations: the coupled differential equations that a metric and fields must satisfy together; a "branch" is one solution path of these equations.
- Primordial dark matter: dark matter thought to have formed in the early universe.
summary.one_liner: A comment arguing that a proposed exact black hole solution sourced by a phantom Dirac-Born-Infeld scalar field, offered as primordial dark matter, fails to satisfy the full field equations across the event horizon.
summary.plain: This is a short critical reply to a earlier paper that claimed to have found a black hole built from a special kind of field, which the earlier work suggested could be a form of primordial dark matter. The author checks the proposed solution against the full set of equations for that field and reports that it does not hold in the region around the horizon, the boundary past which light cannot escape. So, according to this comment, the proposed object is not a valid black hole of that theory.
summary.why: It bears on whether a specific exotic model of dark matter can produce black holes without singularities, a question of interest to people studying black holes and cosmology. The text is only the abstract of a comment, so the details of the calculation and any response from the original authors are not available here.

papers.abstract: We demonstrate that the metric and scalar configuration proposed in Ref.~[1] do not satisfy the complete set of field equations of the Dirac-Born-Infeld (DBI) field theory minimally coupled to general relativity on a radial domain containing the event horizon. The physical DBI branch for this gravitational setup terminates outside the event horizon. Thus, the proposed configuration does not describe a black hole solution of that theory.

papers.title: ER=EPR and IMP wormholes in quantum gravity
papers.label: arXiv:2611.23396v1

summary.background:
- Entanglement: a quantum link between particles that holds even when they are far apart.
- ER=EPR: a conjecture that entanglement (EPR pairs) corresponds to wormholes (Einstein–Rosen bridges).
- General relativity: Einstein's theory where gravity is the curvature of space-time, described by the Einstein equations.
- Cauchy slice: a snapshot of space at one moment, used to set up the initial data for evolving a universe.
- Constant mean curvature: a condition on how a snapshot of space bends, used to make the construction consistent.
- AdS/CFT: a correspondence relating gravity in an anti-de Sitter universe to a quantum field theory on its boundary.
- Perturbation theory: approximating a hard problem by expanding in a small parameter, here Newton's constant G_N.
summary.one_liner: The paper refines the ER=EPR conjecture by building IMP (Isenberg–Mazzeo–Pollack) wormhole solutions to Einstein's equations in AdS/CFT, using the conformal method to set up perturbation theory in quantum gravity, including the limit where Newton's constant G_N is zero.
summary.plain: The paper studies a proposal that two quantum-entangled particles are linked by a tiny wormhole (a shortcut through space-time). It does this by constructing special wormhole-shaped solutions to Einstein's gravity equations that add a handle to a known universe while leaving the data elsewhere unchanged. The authors also set up a way to do calculations in quantum gravity for these backgrounds, both for small effects and beyond small-effect approximations.
summary.why: Connecting entanglement to geometry is an active question in theoretical physics, and the ER=EPR idea is one of the proposals that tries to do this. The text does not state specific results, so its significance beyond the stated construction is unclear from this excerpt alone.

papers.abstract: We analyze and refine the ER=EPR conjecture by studying IMP (Isenberg, Mazzeo and Pollack \cite{Isenberg:2001qe}) wormholes in QFT and quantum gravity, in the AdS/CFT context. IMP wormholes are solutions to the Einstein equations constructed from another general solution of Einstein's equations by gluing a handle on a Cauchy slice with a constant mean curvature, so that the initial data on the slice does not change in the regions away from the handle. This is made possible by using what is called the conformal method. This same method also enables one to recover a well defined perturbation theory in quantum gravity, and particularly for asymptotically AdS spacetimes \cite{Witten:2022xxp}. Thus we construct the perturbation theory on these backgrounds in addition to exploring ER=EPR when $G_{N}=0$, in the limit it is perturbatively small and beyond perturbation theory.

papers.title: On Thermodynamics of AdS Black Holes in Square-Root Nonlinear Electrodynamics
papers.label: arXiv:2611.20162v1

summary.background:
- Black holes can be assigned a temperature, entropy and pressure, using analogies with ordinary thermodynamics.
- Anti-de Sitter (AdS) space is a curved spacetime with negative cosmological constant, often used as a testing ground for these analogies.
- Nonlinear electrodynamics is a modified version of Maxwell's theory of electric and magnetic fields in which the field energy does not simply add up linearly; here the modification has a square-root form.
- P-v criticality: plotting pressure against specific volume, some black holes show a critical point like a liquid-gas transition, with a Van der Waals-type curve.
- Stability and phase transitions describe whether the system stays put or switches between distinct states as conditions change.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes a new charged black hole in anti-de Sitter space, sourced by a square-root nonlinear electrodynamics inspired by exponential Maxwell models, and studies its thermodynamic stability, P-v criticality and phase transitions.
summary.plain: This paper looks at a theoretical model of a black hole, the dense object whose gravity is so strong that light cannot escape. The authors change the rule for how the electric field behaves, using a square-root form inspired by a family of "exponential" versions of Maxwell's electromagnetism. They then treat the black hole like a thermal system with temperature and pressure and check whether it is stable and whether it undergoes phase changes.
summary.why: The authors report that this black hole shows Van der Waals-like behaviour, the same kind of liquid-gas pattern seen in ordinary real gases, without extra correction terms that such comparisons often need. This is a theoretical result, and the text does not say how it bears on observations or other systems, so its wider significance is unclear.

papers.abstract: Inspired by exponential Maxwell models, we propose a new black hole solution in square root nonlinear electrodynamics. Using the analogy between black hole mechanics and thermodynamics, we investigate the corresponding stability, the P-v criticality and the phase transitions. As a result, we find that the obtained black hole exhibits Van der Waals behaviors without additional corrections which typically appear in universal ratio computations.

papers.title: A Gravitomagnetic Bootstrap: from Newtonian gravity to general relativity via localizing rotational and conformal symmetries
papers.label: arXiv:2611.20210v1

summary.background:
- Galilean inertial structure: the rules of motion in Newtonian physics, where straight-line uniform motion defines "inertial" frames.
- Equivalence Principle: the observation that gravity affects all bodies the same way, which lets gravity be treated as a feature of geometry or a local field.
- Localization (gauging) of a symmetry: making a symmetry transformation depend on position and time, which forces a new field to appear to compensate.
- Rotational and conformal (scale) symmetries: rotations of space and changes of length and time units; here they are made local.
- Post-Newtonian approximation: a series of small corrections to Newton's gravity, valid for weak fields and slow speeds, used to test general relativity.
- Special relativity: Einstein's theory of space and time without gravity, which the paper aims to avoid presupposing.
summary.one_liner: The paper argues that localizing rotational inertia and spatial and temporal scaling, on top of the Galilean structure underlying Newtonian gravity, yields a essentially unique theory that matches the first post-Newtonian approximation to general relativity for a suitable choice of a velocity constant and sign.
summary.plain: The paper asks what kind of gravity theory you get if you start from Newton's picture and additionally make rotations and changes of spatial and temporal scale "local", meaning they can vary from place to place, as Einstein did for straight-line motion. The author reports that, under weak assumptions, this construction gives one theory up to a single constant with units of speed and an overall sign. With the right choice of that constant, the theory agrees with the first post-Newtonian (small-correction) approximation to general relativity, offering a route from Newtonian gravity to Einstein's theory without assuming special relativity at the outset.
summary.why: It is a conceptual route to general relativity that does not start from special relativity, which may clarify why gravity has the structure it does. The text does not show how far the approach extends beyond the first post-Newtonian order, so its wider significance is uncertain.

papers.abstract: Newtonian gravity, in the light of the Equivalence Principle, is best understood as a localization of Galilean inertial structure --- or at least, of the part of Galilean inertial structure that defines rectilinear acceleration. I consider what kind of theory can be constructed if we also localize rotational inertia and spatial and temporal scales. The resultant theory, given weak assumptions, is unique up to a constant with the dimensions of velocity and an overall sign. For an appropriate choice of these, it coincides with the first post-Newtonian approximation to general relativity, so that this construction gives a method to bootstrap from Newtonian gravity to general relativity without explicitly presupposing special relativity.
